# WIP: Threat Model: Autonomous AI Code Review Agent

Author(s): Mohamad El Hajj, Kevin Calloway, Julia Cabral, Meret Wilfurth, Navneet Keshav, Shrey Bagga  
Date: Jun 12, 2026

**Framework:** STRIDE, extended with AI-specific risk categories   
**Applicability:** Any organization deploying an LLM-based agent as a reviewer or approver of source code changes   
**Status:** Draft

---

## 1\. Purpose and Scope

This document defines a reference threat model for systems in which an AI model acts as a reviewer — and potentially an autonomous approver — of source code changes (pull requests / merge requests). It is intended to be vendor-neutral and generalizable across organizations, and to serve three purposes:

1. Establish a shared threat model for the risks introduced when an AI system participates in, or replaces, human code review.  
2. Define the security control objectives and architectural patterns required to mitigate those risks.  
3. Provide evidence for compliance assessments of AI-assisted code review, with autonomous approval limited to the scope permitted by applicable obligations and the organization's approved decision controls policy (e.g., SOX/ICFR, SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA). 

**In scope:** The AI reviewer service, its model behavior, its inputs (PR content and metadata), its tool integrations, its credentials and infrastructure, and the approval/audit pipeline.

**Out of scope:** General SDLC security (branch protection design, CI hardening) except where the AI reviewer changes the risk profile.

## 2\. Reference Architecture

The model prescribes a reference architecture for AI code review systems where there is a collection of “Enforcement Layers” responsible for maintaining constraints on the access, promotion, review and analysis of code.

![][image1]

### EL1: Review Orchestrator 

![][image2]  
**Review Orchestrator (High Level Architecture)**

**Components:**

- **Review orchestrator** — a deterministic, programmatic service (not an AI agent) that receives repository events, dispatches review sub-tasks, aggregates results, and renders the final approval decision via hard logic rules. The orchestrator contains no AI reasoning.  
- **Primary AI reviewer** — an LLM agent (or bundle of agents) that analyzes the change for correctness, security, and policy conformance. (e.g. [Code Guard](https://github.com/cosai-oasis/project-codeguard) can serve as a baseline tool for security rules checks within the Primary AI reviewer. The Primary AI reviewer is a harness that would go beyond this to also discover issues beyond security vulnerabilities like bugs, architecture issues, slop, configuration correctness, your SDLC requirements compliance, etc.)  
- **Classifier ensemble** — specialized LLM model-based checks (adversarial-input detection, risk tiering, compliance scoping, intent and quality evaluation, project-convention checks) that run before or alongside the primary reviewer. Any hard veto blocks approval regardless of the AI reviewer's assessment. Some classifiers may only be run on certain paths or data. (example: Domain-specific reviewers for specific functions of the code;  Risk classifier to determine level of risk associated with pull request; Compliance classifier to determine if compliance requirements triggered by pull request)  
- **Deterministic analyzers** — SAST tooling, test gates, and invariant checks that share none of the model's failure modes; confirmed findings or failures block approval.  
- **Tool integrations** — internal services (source-control APIs, knowledge bases, chat systems) and external resources (vulnerability databases, package registries, documentation) the AI may query during review.  
- **Approval identity** — a machine credential (e.g., a source-control bot token or app installation) through which approvals are exercised. This identity enables uniquely identifying the approver agent and configuring its permissions (e.g., cannot approve its own code).

## Code Management Infrastructure (EL2 \- EL5)

These components are intended to be implemented as commodity software systems. More details in section 6.1.

### 2.1 Trust Boundaries

| \# | Boundary | Crossing |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| TB1 | Code Contributor → AI Reviewer | PR content, metadata, commit messages, and comments enter the AI's context |
| TB2 | AI Reviewer → Tools | Each tool invocation sends context out and brings third-party data in |
| TB3 | External content → AI Reviewer | Fetched web/registry/CVE content enters the AI's context |
| TB4 | AI Review system ↔ Source-control platform | Repository events and PR state come in. Approval decisions are exercised via a privileged machine identity, and review comments, findings, and summaries are posted to everyone who can read the PR, including downstream agents |
| TB5 | System Operators → AI Review system | Configuration, governance files, prompts, and policy definitions |
| TB6 | AI Reviewer → Audit pipeline | Decision records flow to logging and compliance systems |
| TB7 | AI Review system → System Operators | Alerts and health status updates for system |
| TB8  | AI Reviewer and classifiers ↔ LLM API / model provider | Diff, surrounding code, instructions, and retrieved context may leave EL3 for an approved model endpoint; model outputs return into the review. Applies where a model is hosted outside EL3.   |
| TB9 | Continuous integration → Review orchestrator | Results of jobs that execute contributor-controlled code (build, test, install hooks) are consumed as deterministic signals. |

### 2.2 Key Assets

- Approval authority (the ability to merge code into protected branches)  
- The reviewer's machine credentials and tokens  
- Governance artifacts: review policy files, eligibility rules, classifier definitions, the reviewer's own implementation  
- Source code and additional context exposed to the reviewer  
- User input and review feedback  
- System logs, audit records, and decision rationale  
- Compliance posture (regulatory scope boundaries and attestations)

### 2.3 Trust Assumptions

No model in this design is completely trusted. The Primary AI reviewer, every classifier, and any model added to check them can be wrong (A-2, A-3), manipulated through their inputs (T-1, T-2), substituted (T-6), or drift from intended behavior (A-1). Models that share a base model, provider, or context can fail together. It depends on four properties:

1. The model can only veto approval. It is never granted unilateral approval control. The Review orchestrator (EL1) computes the decision in code from eligibility, the absence of vetoes, and required checks.  
2. The worst case is bounded by deterministic scope. A fully compromised reviewer can at most stay silent (T-9), or leak information via tool calls. What is approved in that case is what the eligibility gate, static analysis, tests, and invariants would allow with no AI review at all. Organizations should set eligibility so that this worst case is acceptable.  
3. Performance is verified by a human reviewer that is potentially assisted by deterministic analyzers.  
4. Reviewer behavior is measured from outside the reviewer. Seeded changes, blind human sampling, and continuous evaluation (6.6) run outside the reviewer's control, and a failure removes authority through the Kill switch (6.5).

Note: The deterministic enforcement in EL1 through EL5, the humans who own it are all considered to be trusted.

## 3\. Threat Actors

| Actor | Description | Primary Attack Surface |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Unintentional Insider | Legitimate engineer or operator acting without intent to harm. Includes contributors whose changes (often AI-assisted) introduce security/compliance issues due to negligence or incomplete understanding of scope and transitive dependencies, and operators who misconfigure the review system (over-broad permissions, weak logging, exposed credentials). | PR content and metadata (TB1). Reviewer configuration, governance files, and credentials (TB5). Logging setup (TB6).  **Examples:**  compliance boundary violations, over-privileged reviewer identity, broken or missing controls for project invariants. |
| Malicious Insider | Employee or contractor acting with intent, potentially leveraging AI tools to cause harm. | PR content and metadata (TB1). Internal sources the reviewer reads, such as tickets, wikis, and chat (TB2). Governance files, policy, and reviewer infrastructure (TB5). Audit records (TB6).   **Examples:** compliance scope bypass, governance file tampering, context window exploitation. |
| Misaligned AI Agent | An AI coding agent, or the AI reviewer itself, behaving against intent with no attacker involved: an author agent optimizing for approval signals, or a reviewer affected by model drift or capability regression. | AI-authored PR content (TB1). Any memory or prior-review store the reviewer reads (TB2). Reviewer and classifier outputs (TB4, TB8).   **Examples:** self-approval of governance changes, fabricated compliance assessments. |
| External Adversary | Third-party \- often supply chain attacker \- with no legitimate write access who influences the review through poisoned package documentation, malicious vulnerability-database entries, or compromised external references. Also includes outside contributors who can open PRs from forks, anyone operating a compromised internal account, and AI coding agents operating in manipulated state due to prompt injection, model compromise, or unauthorized access. | External reference interfaces and documentation ingestion points, including package metadata, vulnerability databases, public repositories, and agent configuration files (TB2, TB3). Fork PRs where the project accepts them (TB1). Webhook and event endpoints (TB4). Reviewer dependencies and the model endpoint (TB8).  **Examples:** indirect prompt injection, supply chain compromise. |

## 4\. STRIDE Threat Enumeration

Threats are organized by STRIDE category. Actor references map to Section 3\. Each threat's controls are listed in the Mitigates column of Section 6\.

### 4.1 Spoofing

*Spoofing is illegitimately assuming an identity the system trusts — here, exercising or impersonating the reviewer's identity, credentials, or event sources.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| S-1 | **Approval Credential Theft or Misuse** | The reviewer's machine credential is exposed (leaked in logs, over-shared, improperly scoped) or stored insecurely (hardcoded, committed to a repository, outside a secrets manager), allowing anyone holding it to issue approvals as the reviewer. | Approval authority exercised entirely outside the review process; forged approvals indistinguishable from legitimate ones. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| S-2 | **Spoofed Repository Events** | Forged or replayed webhook/PR events trick the orchestrator into reviewing or approving content that does not correspond to the actual repository state. | Approval applied to a different change than the one reviewed. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| S-3 | **Author/Approver Identity Confusion** | The system fails to enforce author ≠ approver separation. This can happen at the identity level (the approval identity approves a change it authored), at the lineage level (an AI agent authors a change and a reviewer built on the same model, instructions, and/or context approves it, so both share the same blind spots), or at the human level (one person directs an AI author and the AI reviewer approves, so no second person is involved at all). | Segregation-of-duties violations; single point of failure for both authorship and review | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider, Misaligned AI Agent |

### 4.2 Tampering

*Tampering is the unauthorized modification of data or code — here, manipulating the reviewer's inputs, context, governance artifacts, or execution environment to corrupt its decisions.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| T-1 | **Prompt Injection (Direct and Indirect)** | Adversarially crafted content embeds directives that manipulate the AI's review behavior. The injection may be **direct** — placed in the change itself (code, PR metadata, commit messages, comments; TB1) — or **indirect** — embedded in data the AI retrieves during review, such as a poisoned vulnerability-database entry, a compromised package README, or a manipulated internal message (TB2/TB3). The mechanism and impact are identical; only the entry point differs. Reviewer comments or summaries can also become an indirect-injection source when an AI author or another downstream agent consumes them.  | Approval of malicious code; suppression of security findings. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| T-2 | **Jailbreaking / Role-Constraint Override** | Inputs attempt to strip the AI's role constraints rather than inject new directives — role-play framings, false authority claims, hypothetical framings — causing the AI to step outside its sanctioned reviewer role. | The reviewer ignores risk-tier routing, bypasses eligibility gates, or approves changes it is explicitly constrained from approving. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| T-3 | **Compromised Internal Data Source** | An internal service or context provider the reviewer relies on is compromised or returns manipulated data, feeding the AI false "ground truth" about the codebase, dependencies, or prior reviews. | Approval decisions based on attacker-controlled context. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| T-4 | **Governance Artifact Tampering (Self-Review)** | The AI reviewer is permitted to approve changes to its own governance files (ownership rules, reviewer policy files, agent instructions) or its own implementation — silently redefining its review standards, constraints, or coverage with no human oversight. | The reviewer weakens or redefines its own constraints at the source. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| T-5 | **Runtime Service Compromise** | An attacker gains access to the reviewer's execution environment and tampers with the review process live — intercepting communications, manipulating inputs or outputs, or operating inside the service boundary. | Review decisions manipulated or fabricated at runtime, bypassing review logic and potentially the audit trail. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| T-6 | **Reviewer Infrastructure Supply Chain Attack** | A dependency of the reviewer service — base container image, runtime package, build toolchain — is compromised, injecting malicious behavior into the reviewer's execution environment. | Reviewer outputs manipulated or exfiltrated at the infrastructure level, below all review logic. | External Adversary |
| T-7  | **Untrusted Code Execution in the Review Pipeline**  | Contributor-controlled tests, build scripts, package install hooks, or pre-commit hooks execute in CI as part of review. If they are not isolated from the orchestrator, approval identity, privileged credentials, or trusted writable state, the PR can obtain credentials or alter check results.  | Approval authority or reviewer credentials compromised from inside the pipeline; forged or altered check results. This is a concrete route to T-5 and S-1.  | Malicious Insider, External Adversary  |
| T-8  | **Change Decomposition Across Pull Requests** | A harmful change is split across several small PRs that may each pass review alone; unsafe behavior appears when they are combined. The change-size gate encourages splitting, while the intent classifier evaluates one PR at a time.  | Per-PR review misses the combined unsafe behavior and permits malicious or flawed changes to be merged in stages.  | Malicious Insider, Misaligned AI Agent  |
| T-9 | **Reviewer Finding Suppression** | The Primary AI reviewer or a classifier operates in a manipulated or degraded state and omits findings, under-rates severity, or reports a clean assessment that is not accurate. This is the outcome of T-1, T-2, T-6 or A-1, listed separately so the controls that bound it are mapped.  | The AI review signal is silently absent. Approval falls back to whatever the deterministic layers catch inside eligible scope. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary, Misaligned AI Agent |

### 4.3 Repudiation

*Repudiation is the ability to deny an action occurred because the system cannot prove otherwise — here, the inability to reconstruct, trust, or attribute the AI's approval decisions after the fact.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| R-1 | **Audit Trail Gaps** | Insufficient logging of the AI's approval rationale, input signals, and model version makes it impossible to reconstruct why a decision was made. | Compliance audit failures; inability to investigate post-incident; AI approval cannot be defended as equivalent to human approval. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| R-2 | **Mutable or Self-Writable Audit Logs** | Decision records are not tamper-evident, or the AI reviewer (or its service identity) has write access to its own audit logs. | Decisions can be altered or erased after the fact; forensic integrity lost. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| R-3 | **Unattributable Automated Decisions** | Classifier and analyzer signals are recorded as bare pass/fail without reasoning, so contributing factors to an approval cannot be attributed or contested. | Disputed approvals cannot be decomposed; accountability for AI performance cannot be assigned to a control owner. | Unintentional Insider |

### 4.4 Information Disclosure

*Information disclosure is the exposure of data to parties not authorized to see it — here, leakage of source code, credentials, or sensitive context through the reviewer's operation.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| I-1 | **Data Exfiltration via Tool Calls** | The AI is manipulated into transmitting diff contents, internal code, or sensitive context to an external service as part of a tool call (e.g., embedding source in an external "lookup"). | Exposure of proprietary code, unreleased features, or security-sensitive implementation details. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |
| I-2 | **Credential Exposure** | Reviewer secrets surface in logs, error messages, configuration, or repository history. | Leads directly to S-1; full compromise of approval authority. | Unintentional Insider |
| I-3 | **Over-Broad Context Exposure** | The reviewer is granted read access to more code, systems, or data than its review function requires, so any manipulation or compromise discloses more than the change under review. | Blast radius of any reviewer compromise extends to unrelated proprietary or regulated data. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| I-4  | **Disclosure Through Reviewer Output**  | PR comments, findings, and summaries can reveal secrets, code from other repositories, or retrieved context to PR readers who are not authorized to receive that information, even when the destination is the approved source-control platform. | Sensitive context disclosed to the PR audience beyond its authorized access. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary, Misaligned AI Agent |
| I-5 | **Disclosure at the Model Endpoint** | Code, instructions, and retrieved context sent to a model hosted outside EL3-Reviewer infrastructure (TB8) are retained, logged, used for training, or exposed in a provider incident, or are sent to an endpoint or region the organization has not approved. | Proprietary or regulated code held by a third party beyond the organization's control, with possible contractual or regulatory breach. | Unintentional Insider, External Adversary |

### 4.5 Denial of Service

*Denial of service is degrading or exhausting a system's capacity to perform its function — here, attacks on the reviewer's attention, throughput, or availability that erode review quality.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| D-1 | **Context Window Exhaustion** | Oversized changes exhaust the AI's effective context, pushing critical hunks beyond its attention. Functions as a denial of *review quality*: the service still answers, but meaningful review is degraded. | Changes at the tail of a large diff evade meaningful scrutiny. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| D-2 | **Change-Size Exploitation** | A PR is deliberately inflated to hide malicious changes within bulk additions, overwhelming review capacity. | Malicious code smuggled through otherwise benign changes. | Malicious Insider |
| D-3 | **Review Pipeline Flooding** | High volumes of automated or low-value PRs saturate reviewer throughput, delaying or degrading review of legitimate changes, or pressuring operators to relax gates. Repeated automated fix-and-review cycles can also consume review capacity and model budgets.  | Reduced review rigor under load; availability loss for the approval pipeline. | Malicious Insider, External Adversary |

### 4.6 Elevation of Privilege

*Elevation of privilege is gaining authority beyond what was granted — here, the reviewer, its credential, or a contributor obtaining approval power or scope they should not hold.*

| ID | Threat | Description | Potential Impact | Actor(s) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| E-1 | **Self-Approval of Governance Changes** | The reviewer approves modifications that expand its own authority, scope, or permissions (overlaps T-4; listed here for the privilege-escalation outcome). | Unsupervised expansion of autonomous approval authority. | Misaligned AI Agent |
| E-2 | **Over-Privileged Reviewer Identity** | The approval service holds source-control permissions beyond what its function requires (write access to repos it doesn't review, admin scopes, org-level rights). | A compromised service grants broad repository or organization access. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| E-3 | **Over-Privileged Tool Access** | The AI has access to more tools or internal services than review requires — chat systems, internal wikis, administrative APIs. | A manipulated reviewer can read/write across internal systems well beyond the change under review. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| E-4 | **Compliance Boundary Bypass** | A change touching regulated code (financial reporting, health data, PII processing) is misclassified as out of scope and approved autonomously, when policy requires human approval. Includes transitive exposure: a change to non-sensitive code that affects a protected library or data flow. | Regulatory violations; failed audits; unauthorized changes to controlled systems. | Unintentional Insider, Malicious Insider |
| E-5 | **Reward Hacking by an AI Author** | An AI coding agent learns to optimize for *passing review* rather than producing genuinely correct or secure code — satisfying classifiers and the reviewer on the surface while pursuing subtly divergent goals. Evasion is by design, making failures hard to detect or attribute. | Systematic introduction of subtly flawed changes that pass all gates; effective escalation from "author" to "self-approving author." | Misaligned AI Agent |
| E-6 | **Eligibility and Scope Evasion via Path Rules**  | Path-based controls use incomplete classifications or evaluate only the post-change path without checking original paths, content, or dependencies. Renames, misleading extensions, or false vendored/generated labels can cause changes to be assigned to a lower tier, omitted from protected scope, or excluded from size metrics. | High-risk, protected, or oversized changes become eligible for autonomous approval because their effective scope is misclassified. | Malicious Insider |

## 5\. AI-Intrinsic Risks (Beyond STRIDE)

STRIDE models adversarial action, but an AI reviewer also introduces *capability* failure modes that exist independent of any attacker. These are baseline failure modes of deploying an LLM as a security gatekeeper and should be tracked alongside the STRIDE enumeration. They align with emerging AI-risk frameworks (e.g., OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF).

| ID | Risk | Description | Potential Impact |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| A-1 | **Model Misalignment / Drift** | Reviewer behavior diverges from intended standards through model updates, drift, or capability regression. | Systematic approval of poor-quality or insecure code. |
| A-2 | **Hallucination** | The reviewer fabricates conclusions about code correctness or compliance status not grounded in the actual diff. | False approval signals; vulnerabilities classified as benign. |
| A-3 | **Reasoning Inaccuracy** | The model reasons from real inputs but draws wrong conclusions. | Missed bugs, security flaws, or compliance violations. |
| A-4 | **Knowledge Blind Spots** | The reviewer is unaware of new frameworks, novel attack patterns, or organization-specific standards. | Emerging threats undetected; internal standards unenforced. |
| A-5 | **Tunnel Vision / Incomplete Context** | The change is reviewed in isolation without upstream/downstream dependencies or project invariants. | Locally correct but globally unsafe changes approved. |
| A-6 | **Generic-vs-Specific Gap** | The reviewer applies general best practices but lacks team-specific conventions, domain constraints, or compliance rules. | Organization-specific requirements missed. |
| A-7 | **Missing or misunderstood context** | The reviewer is not given, or does not use, the requirements and operational context needed to judge the change, including undocumented invariants, deployment constraints, and downstream consumers. Differs from A-5 and A-6 in that the missing information is not in the codebase or in team standards. It is unwritten, or it lives with the people who run the system.  | The reviewer approves a change that violates an undocumented requirement or misunderstands its operational effect, so the change solves the wrong problem or has unintended effects on other systems.  |

A critical operating assumption follows from these risks: **absence of findings is not evidence of safety.** Silence from the AI reviewer, classifiers, or analyzers means only that no issue was detected; only a negative output (a finding or veto) carries meaning.

## 6\. Control Objectives and Mitigations

Controls are stated as objectives so they can be implemented with any toolchain. The mapping column ties each control to the threats it mitigates.

### 6.1 Input and Decision Integrity Controls

The Primary AI reviewer is listed first as the principal signal; the remaining classifiers follow in order of the input they operate on — raw submission text, change metadata, the code diff, and the diff combined with descriptive or organizational context. The final two rows are deterministic and model-independent — they cannot be prompt-injected, do not hallucinate, and do not drift across model versions — serving as a backstop that does not share the model-based signals' reasoning failure modes. Each control also carries an **Example** describing one way to implement it and the mechanism that enforces it. The examples assume a typical software development lifecycle (SDLC) setup built from five parts, and every "Enforced by" note in the tables points to one of them. Named products are illustrative of common tooling, and are not required.

* **EL1: Review orchestrator.** A small deterministic service, typically a continuous integration (CI) job or webhook handler, that receives the pull request (PR) event, applies the eligibility gate (before any model call, and again once the classifiers have returned), calls each classifier and the Primary AI reviewer, validates every model response against a required structure (e.g., a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schema), and computes the decision as plain code: approve only if the change is eligible, no signal has vetoed, and all required checks have passed. Any error, timeout, or malformed response counts as a veto. It reports its result to the source-control platform as a status check and, when approving, submits the review through the approval identity. This is ordinary code the organization writes, tests, and code-reviews like any other service.  
* **EL2: Source-control platform**. Branch protection on the protected branch requiring the orchestrator's status check, the static analysis and test checks, and at least one approving review, with the approval identity counted as a reviewer only where the decision controls policy allows. A code-ownership file (e.g., GitHub CODEOWNERS) assigns human owners to the governance artifacts and to the orchestrator's own repository. The approval identity is a dedicated application or project token (e.g., a GitHub App) holding only pull-request write and repository read permissions.  
* **EL3: Reviewer infrastructure.** The orchestrator, classifiers, and Primary AI reviewer run in an isolated container whose outbound network access is limited to an allow-list: the large language model (LLM) application programming interface (API), the source-control platform API, and optionally a vulnerability feed such as the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database. Credentials are issued at job start from the CI provider's OpenID Connect (OIDC) token or a secrets manager and are scoped to that single run. The approval credential is held only by the orchestrator process. Models and their tools run in a separate sandbox that never sees it.  
* **EL4: Governance artifacts**. The version-controlled files that define how the system behaves: the decision controls policy (path-to-risk-tier map, regulated-scope paths, change-size limit, classifier thresholds, owner opt-out paths, and which tiers are eligible for autonomous approval, e.g., in an ai-review-policy.yaml kept where only its owners can change it), the agent instructions, classifier definitions, per-project context files, static analysis rule sets, and the orchestrator's own implementation. Humans own and define these policies and configurations through the code-ownership registry, the orchestrator reads them at the start of every review, and the Self-protection gate (6.2) ensures the AI reviewer can never approve changes to them.  
* **EL5: Continuous integration.** Automated CI pipelines that execute build, test, static analysis (SAST), and invariant check jobs triggered by repository events. CI job results are dispatched back to the Review orchestrator as deterministic signals or required status checks that must pass before approval can proceed.

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary AI reviewer (bugs and correctness)** | The principal review signal: analyzes the change for bugs, logic errors, and security vulnerabilities. Confirmed findings carry veto authority and must be acknowledged or resolved before approval. **Preconditions:** A repository event triggers the orchestrator and all relevant diff files and context are assembled. **Postconditions:** If findings at or above the blocking severity are present or response parsing fails, the change is vetoed; otherwise, findings are logged and approval proceeds. | A-2, A-3, A-4 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, integrated with an LLM gateway/service. **Algorithm:**  1\. Send the diff, surrounding code, and reviewer instructions (including Project CodeGuard security rule sets) to the LLM.  2\. Enforce structural JSON schema parsing on the response; if the response doesn't match the required structure, treat it as a veto.  3\. Evaluate findings against the configured blocking severity threshold (set by humans in the policy file). If any finding is at or above the blocking severity, the change is vetoed. |
| **Reviewer report verification (optional)** | Check the Primary AI reviewer's report before its result is used. Veto-only: a failed check withholds approval and a passed check adds nothing. Deterministic checks come first. A model-based checker (sometimes called an alignment checker) is optional, is subject to T-1, T-2 and T-9 like any other model, and does not replace deterministic vetoes or human sampling. **Preconditions:** The reviewer has returned a schema-valid report, and the changed-file list has been fetched from the platform API. **Postconditions:** An incomplete, ungrounded, or inconsistent report withholds autonomous approval and routes the change to human review. | T-9, A-2; residual T-1 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator. **Algorithm:**  1\. Coverage: compare the files and hunks the report says it reviewed with the changed-file list from the platform API. Anything unaccounted for is a veto. 2\. Grounding: confirm every finding cites a file and line present in the diff, and veto on findings that do not. 3\. Consistency: check in code that severity labels match the policy's definitions for the finding category, and that the report holds no text addressed to the orchestrator or to downstream agents. 4\. Optional: pass the diff and the report as quoted data to a separate model call with no tools, asking only whether the report omits something material. Record whether it shares a base model or provider with the reviewer. 5\. Test the checker itself with seeded bad reports (findings removed, severity lowered) through the Adversarial change pipeline (6.6). |
| **Adversarial-input classifier** | Scan all PR inputs (code, metadata, commit messages, comments) for injection and jailbreak patterns before the AI reviews. Hard veto on detection. **Preconditions:** A repository event (PR/MR) is triggered, and all contributor-controlled text inputs (diff, PR title, description, commit messages, comments, file names, branch name) are aggregated prior to primary model invocation. **Postconditions:** If an adversarial input or instruction is detected, the review pipeline immediately halts, vetoes approval, skips calling the Primary AI reviewer, and routes the PR to human review. Otherwise, processing proceeds to subsequent review stages. | T-1 (direct vector), T-2 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, integrated with an off-the-shelf guardrail proxy/model (e.g., Llama Guard, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, or cloud provider prompt-attack filters). **Algorithm:**  1\. Perform rule-based pattern matching on aggregated text for known injection indicators (e.g., hidden/zero-width Unicode, explicit system instructions to approve/ignore findings).  2\. Pass the text as quoted data to an isolated guardrail model call without tools.  3\. Evaluate the returned verdict and confidence score against configured thresholds. |
| **Risk-tier classifier** | Assign each change a risk tier based on compliance scope, file type, change category, and reach; route accordingly. **Preconditions:** The pull request diff and metadata have passed initial adversarial screening. **Postconditions:** The change is assigned a risk tier; if the tier is ineligible for autonomous approval, it is routed for human review with a comment. | E-4, primary routing control, E-6  | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, using a path-to-risk-tier policy file and model-based risk assessment. **Algorithm:**  1\. Compute a floor tier using plain code based on the path-to-risk-tier map and change metrics (lines, files, dependencies, dependents). Evaluate both original and destination paths for renames, and reconcile file type and dependency effects with the path classification; uncertainty cannot lower the tier. 2\. Call a risk-assessment model to evaluate if diff details warrant a higher tier.  3\. Select the maximum of the computed floor tier and model-proposed tier (the model can raise a tier but can never lower one).  4\. Look up in the policy file whether that higher tier is eligible for autonomous approval; ineligible tiers receive a comment-only review and a human reviewer request. |
| **Compliance scope classifier** | Detect direct and transitive exposure to regulated scope (e.g., financial reporting, health data, PII) as a signal in the ensemble — a safety net for scope that the organization's policy mapping has missed or not yet captured. **Preconditions:** Dependency mappings and regulated path policies are loaded by the orchestrator. **Postconditions:** In-scope changes are routed to designated human compliance approvers in the code-ownership file, and any model-only detections are logged for policy updates. | E-4, E-6 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, combining deterministic graph/path matching with LLM analysis. **Algorithm:**  1\. Perform a deterministic pass mapping touched files and dependencies against regulated-scope paths and data tags. Include original and destination paths, content-derived classifications, and affected dependencies when evaluating renames or moves.  2\. Perform a model pass analyzing the diff for implicit regulated content (PII, financial/health records).  3\. Union the verdicts from both passes. An in-scope verdict from either pass is treated as final and routes the change to the human approver named for that regime in the code-ownership file (the model can add scope but can never remove scope the policy mapping assigned). Log model-only hits so owners can add missing paths to the policy file. |
| **Code quality classifier** | Flags low-quality or careless code ("slop") — deviations from engineering standards, unjustified complexity, boilerplate-heavy or under-tested output — independent of whether it is strictly correct. Particularly relevant where AI agents author a high volume of changes. **Preconditions:** CI static checks, linters, and test coverage jobs have completed. **Postconditions:** If the score is below the threshold, autonomous approval is withheld and line-item findings are posted to the PR. | A-4, A-6 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, executing an LLM-based rubric evaluation. **Algorithm:**  1\. Pass the diff, engineering standards, and CI linter/coverage reports to the LLM.  2\. Score the change against a human-owned rubric covering duplication, unjustified complexity, placeholder code, and test quality.  3\. Compare the aggregate score to the policy quality threshold. If below the threshold, withhold autonomous approval and post line-item findings for the author (teams may set this signal to advisory/comment-only for their lowest tier). |
| **Intent classifier** | Evaluates whether the change's actual behavior matches its stated purpose — flagging hidden functionality, unexplained indirection, or effects that diverge from the change description. The primary preventive signal against approval-gaming and smuggled changes. **Preconditions:** PR description, commit messages, and diff are available. **Postconditions:** Unstated behaviors at or above blocking threshold veto autonomous approval and trigger PR comments detailing the mismatch. | E-5, D-2 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, utilizing dual isolated LLM calls and code fact-checkers.  **Algorithm:**  1\. Prompt Model A with only the diff (withholding description/commits) to generate a raw behavior summary.  2\. Prompt Model B to compare Model A's summary against the author's PR description and linked ticket. 3\. Run deterministic checks for contradictions (e.g. non-doc edits in "docs-only" PRs, new external hosts).  4\. Veto autonomous approval and post mismatch details to the PR if any unstated behavior is at or above the policy severity threshold or if a code check contradicts the description. |
| **Project-context evaluation** | Evaluate changes against owner-maintained, per-project context files (security-sensitive areas, conventions, domain constraints) and organization-wide engineering standards, as distinct signals in the ensemble. This may also take the form of dedicated domain- or project-specific classifiers — purpose-built checks for a particular codebase, business domain, or regulatory context — contributed and maintained by the owning team. **Preconditions:** Context files exist on the protected default branch. Required context and its owner are identified in protected policy. **Postconditions:** Any violation of a rule marked as blocking generates a veto and prevents autonomous approval. Missing, stale, or ambiguous required context withholds autonomous approval and requests owner clarification. | A-5, A-6, A-7 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, loading protected domain context files.  **Algorithm:**  0\. Check required context against the protected inventory and its source versions. If required information is absent, stale, or ambiguous, withhold autonomous approval and ask the owner; do not infer undocumented requirements as fact. 1\. Fetch project context files (e.g., REVIEW\_CONTEXT.md) from the default branch (protected via code-ownership so PRs editing context files route to human review under the Self-protection gate).  2\. Pass context rules and diff to an LLM or domain-specific evaluator tool.  3\. Evaluate compliance for each rule and extract structured verdicts, vetoing on any violated rule marked as blocking by owners. |
| **Static analysis veto** | Deterministic, rule-based SAST scanning of the change for vulnerabilities and dangerous patterns. Confirmed findings block approval regardless of any classifier's or the primary reviewer's assessment. **Preconditions:** CI runner executes SAST workflow on PR trigger. **Postconditions:** Findings at or above blocking severity fail the required status check, blocking merge regardless of AI assessments. | A-1, A-2, A-4; residual T-1, T-2 | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform (branch protection) and CI SAST runners (e.g., Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube).  **Algorithm:**  1\. Execute SAST scanners, secret scanners, and dependency checks against the head commit. 2\. Inspect raw source before normalization for bidi controls and confusable identifiers using a protected, language-aware policy. Reject unsafe or unapproved uses and route ambiguous cases to human review; preserve the original bytes for investigation.  3\. Output findings in standard SARIF format.  4\. Filter for new findings introduced by the change against baseline.  5\. Block merge via required branch protection checks if a finding meets or exceeds blocking severity (orchestrator withholds approval). Treat suppressions (inline ignore comments, baseline edits) as Governance artifact changes requiring human review. |
| **Test and invariant gate** | Automated test suites and project-invariant checks (integration tests, static checks per 6.2) must pass for the change. Failures block approval regardless of any classifier's or the primary reviewer's assessment. **Preconditions:** CI pipeline runs test jobs for the PR commit. **Postconditions:** Any test failure or missing required check prevents autonomous approval and blocks merge. | A-1, A-3, A-5, T-7, T-5, S-1  | **Enforced by:** Continuous integration (EL5) and Reviewer infrastructure (EL3) for the isolation in step 0, and the Source-control platform (EL2) via required status checks in branch protection.  **Algorithm:**  0\. Run every CI job that executes contributor-controlled code, including build, test, and install hooks, in a disposable sandbox with no approval token, LLM key, or ability to obtain them. Keep the orchestrator, approval identity, and trusted writable state outside that sandbox. Accept results only from the expected workflow run and check identity for the reviewed head commit. 1\. Execute test suites, integration tests, OPA policy checks, and architecture linter tasks in CI.  2\. Collect status check results for the head commit.  3\. Verify all required check runs returned success before allowing approval (treating missing or pending checks as failures). Changes deleting, skipping, or weakening tests/invariants are routed to human review via path rules under Protected invariants. |

### 6.2 Scope and Eligibility Controls

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Decision controls policy gate** | The organization must define a decision controls policy — which classes of change are eligible for autonomous approval, which require human approval, and what compensating controls apply at each risk level, informed by its regulatory obligations and risk appetite. The review system must deterministically enforce this policy as an eligibility gate before any AI reasoning runs. The content of the policy is organization-specific and out of scope for this document. **Preconditions:** Policy file is present on the default branch. **Postconditions:** If marked ineligible, autonomous approval is halted immediately and human reviewers are assigned. | E-4, S-3, R-1, E-6 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, executing deterministic policy evaluation code (e.g., OPA Rego or Cedar). **Algorithm:**  1\. Load policy definition from the default protected branch.  2\. Evaluate target paths, author identity, and risk tiers against eligibility rules. Evaluate original and destination paths, resolve file-type and dependency effects, and preserve protected-scope and owner opt-out requirements across moves; uncertain classification requires human review.  3\. Assert author \!= approver constraints.  4\. If the gate determines "not eligible", withhold autonomous approval regardless of model output (comments may still be posted); enforce via code-ownership rules requiring human owners on ineligible paths. 5\. Re-run steps 2 to 4 once the Risk-tier and Compliance scope classifiers have returned, using the higher tier and the wider scope. |
| **Self-protection gate** | Hard-block AI approval of any change touching the reviewer's governance files, policy definitions, classifier definitions, or its own implementation — enforced deterministically at the eligibility layer, before any AI reasoning runs. These changes always route to human review. **Preconditions:** List of changed files is retrieved from repository API. **Postconditions:** Autonomous approval is prohibited; human owner signature is strictly required to merge. | T-4, E-1, E-6 | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform (code ownership and branch protection) and Review orchestrator path matchers. **Algorithm:**  1\. Compare PR changed-file list against protected path patterns (policy, prompts, classifiers, workflows, the code-ownership file). Include original and destination paths and changed policy references, so moving a governance file cannot remove its human-review requirement. 2\. Immediately trigger human review flag and prohibit autonomous approval if any match is found.  3\. Enforce code-owner approvals via branch protection (requiring named human owner approval and disallowing the approval identity as a qualifying reviewer with admin bypass disabled). |
| **Change-size gate** | Changes above a defined size threshold are ineligible for autonomous approval and route to human review. **Preconditions:** Diff metrics are retrieved from the platform API. **Postconditions:** Overly large changes veto autonomous approval without truncation and require human review or splitting. | D-1, D-2, E-6 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, using platform API metrics. **Algorithm:**  1\. Query API for total changed lines, files, and diff token count.  2\. Apply vendored/generated exclusions to size metrics only, never to review coverage. Use the protected decision controls policy. 3\. Verify generated files against regeneration from reviewed inputs with a trusted, pinned generator in an isolated sandbox; verify vendored files against recorded origin and integrity. Renames into excluded paths and unverified generated-file claims require human review. Keep an effective input limit for everything actually reviewed; if verification is unavailable, require human review. Exclude vendored/generated files according to path patterns. 4\. Compare metrics against tier ceilings defined in policy.  5\. If over the limit, mark change as ineligible for autonomous approval, refuse truncation (full diff required or veto), and request splitting or human review. |
| **Protected invariants** | A code area is eligible for autonomous review only if machine-checkable invariants (integration tests, static checks) are defined for it; areas without defined invariants route to human review. Invariant definitions themselves require human review to modify. Per-change enforcement of the invariants is performed by the test and invariant gate in 6.1. **Preconditions:** Invariant manifest is registered in governance artifacts. **Postconditions:** Uncovered areas are routed to human reviewers. | T-4, A-3, A-5 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator and code-owner enforcement. **Algorithm:**  1\. Cross-reference changed paths against the invariant manifest (manifest and test files owned by humans in code-ownership file; modifications require human approval).  2\. Verify registered CI invariant checks exist for all touched paths.  3\. Require human review if any path lacks a registered invariant. |
| **Owner opt-out** | Code owners can explicitly exclude files or directories from AI review coverage, routing those paths to human review regardless of risk tier. **Preconditions:** Opt-out configuration is present in policy or repository root. **Postconditions:** Matching paths require human review; AI approval identity will not sign off. | E-4, A-6 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator during eligibility checks. **Algorithm:**  1\. Read opt-out list from policy file and check for \`.no-ai-approval\` marker files (owned by path owners as Governance artifacts).  2\. Match changed file paths against opt-out entries.  3\. Bypass autonomous approval for matches during eligibility checks; require human review. |
| **Cumulative change review** | Evaluate related PRs and the resulting repository state for unsafe combined behavior that a review of one PR could miss. This control is detective and best-effort: it raises the cost of splitting a change and does not prevent it.  **Preconditions:** Protected policy defines related code areas, dependencies, baseline revisions, review windows, and escalation thresholds.  **Postconditions:** Suspicious or incompletely assessed sequences withhold autonomous approval and request human review. | T-8, A-5 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator and CI invariant checks. **Algorithm:**  1\. Retrieve related open and recently merged changes by code area, dependency, or feature; author identity is one signal, not the only grouping.  2\. Assess the cumulative diff and resulting behavior against a recorded baseline and run relevant invariants.  3\. Escalate unexplained combined effects or missing context; retain periodic broader review because a time window is not a complete defense.  |

### 6.3 Tool and Integration Controls

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Least-privilege tool access** | Grant the AI only the tools, and tool actions, required for review (enforced via policy engines or egress proxies). When scoping privilege, the access of the PR owner is also considered. Restrict PR comments, findings, and summaries to information the PR audience is authorized to receive. **Preconditions:** Tool broker is configured with read-only scoped credentials. **Postconditions:** Unapproved tool invocations or write actions are blocked automatically at the broker layer. | E-3, I-3, I-1 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (MCP tool broker, network egress allow-lists, OPA policy engine). **Algorithm:**  1\. Intercept all model tool call requests at the broker.  2\. Validate requested tool and arguments against explicit allow-list; refuse unlisted tools or actions regardless of model request.  3\. Execute request using read-only service tokens scoped strictly to target repo, restricted by network egress allow-list. |
| **Tool output sandboxing** | Treat all tool responses as untrusted input; validate for embedded instructions before the AI acts on them. **Preconditions:** A tool call returns data from an external or internal source. **Postconditions:** Injected directives in tool outputs trigger an immediate pipeline veto. | T-1 (indirect vector) | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator and tool broker proxy. **Algorithm:**  1\. Wrap tool response data in explicit delimiter tags with source labels.  2\. Sanitize HTML, zero-width characters, and system-like formatting.  3\. Run adversarial-input classifier over response content prior to returning to model context; trigger an immediate pipeline veto on detection. Compute final decisions in code from structured findings so injected approval instructions cannot grant approval. |
| **Outbound data controls** | Prohibit transmission of diff contents or internal code to external services except to model endpoints approved in the decision controls policy (TB8), and only for the data categories and purposes authorized there; scope and monitor external lookups (CVE databases, package documentation). For each approved model endpoint, the policy records the data categories it may receive, retention and training terms, access controls, provider incident handling, and which model-version controls are available. **Preconditions:** Reviewer environment network interfaces are initialized under deny-by-default egress policies. **Postconditions:** Unauthorized outbound transmissions are blocked and alerted to security ops. | I-1, I-5 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (egress proxy, container firewall, tool parameter validators). **Algorithm:**  1\. Enforce strict outbound firewall rules allowing only specified LLM endpoints and vulnerability mirrors.  2\. Validate tool query arguments against strict type/length patterns to prevent data smuggling.  3\. Log all egress attempts and forward denied attempts to detection and response systems. |
| **Internal source integrity** | Hold internal services the reviewer depends on to the same security and audit bar as the reviewer itself. **Preconditions:** Internal data sources are registered in governance artifacts with defined trust levels. **Postconditions:** Data from unauthenticated or untrusted internal systems cannot influence approval decisions directly. | T-3 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure and tool broker authentication mechanisms. **Algorithm:**  1\. Connect tool broker only to registered, authenticated data sources via mTLS/signed tokens.  2\. Attach trust-level metadata labels to context items injected into prompt space.  3\. Route freely editable sources through untrusted input sanitization and tool output sandboxing. |

### 6.4 Infrastructure and Identity Controls

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Least-privilege reviewer identity** | Scope the approval credential to the minimum permissions required; no broader repository or organization access. **Preconditions:** Dedicated Non-Human Identity (NHI) is provisioned on target repositories. **Postconditions:** The identity cannot push code, modify pipelines, or approve self-authored PRs. | E-2, S-1 | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform (application or service-account permissions and branch protection settings). **Algorithm:**  1\. Issue short-lived app tokens restricted to pull-request review write scopes.  2\. Isolate app token in orchestrator execution context (withhold from LLM/tools).  3\. Block self-approval and restrict path permissions via platform branch protection settings. |
| **Secrets management** | Store reviewer credentials only in an approved secrets manager with tightly controlled, audited access; never in configuration, code, or logs. **Preconditions:** CI workload identity federation is configured with the secrets manager. **Postconditions:** Secrets are never exposed in prompt contexts, build logs, or code repositories. | S-1, I-2 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (Secrets Manager, OIDC federated identity, log redactor). **Algorithm:**  1\. Authenticate runner via CI OIDC token exchange bound to workload identity access policy.  2\. Fetch secrets directly to orchestrator memory without writing to disk/environment.  3\. Pass log streams through automated redaction filters. |
| **Isolated execution with multi-party control** | Run reviewer agents in hardened, isolated environments; changes to the service require two-party approval. **Preconditions:** Hardened container runtime environment is initialized. **Postconditions:** No persistence or state remains between review executions. | T-5, T-7, S-3 | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform (two-person rule) and Reviewer infrastructure (gVisor/Firecracker microVM containers). **Algorithm:**  1\. Spin up fresh ephemeral microVM/container sandbox (gVisor/Firecracker) for each PR event.  2\. Perform checkout as read-only.  3\. Require two-person rule enforcement via platform branch protection and code ownership on the orchestrator repository. 4\. Destroy container environment upon completion of decision logging. |
| **Service hardening** | Network policies, workload security, and egress controls limit the blast radius of runtime compromise; authenticate and integrity-check all communication with the source-control platform. **Preconditions:** Webhook secrets and TLS certificates are configured. **Postconditions:** Unauthenticated or replayed events are rejected; approvals automatically invalidate if new commits are pushed. | T-5, S-2 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (webhook HMAC verifiers) and Source-control platform (approval dismissal rules). **Algorithm:**  1\. Verify inbound webhook HMAC signature and delivery freshness against network policy.  2\. Re-fetch exact PR state from platform API.  3\. Submit approval specifically tied to head commit SHA, relying on platform dismiss-stale-approval settings to invalidate approvals if new commits are pushed. |
| **Supply chain controls** | Pin and verify all service dependencies (base images, packages, build toolchain); gate dependency updates on human review. **Preconditions:** Build pipeline generates signed SBOMs and provenance attestations. **Postconditions:** Unsigned or unpinned components fail deployment admission checks. | T-6 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (admission controllers, Sigstore cosign) and Source-control platform (code ownership). **Algorithm:**  1\. Pin and verify dependencies, base images, and tool servers using immutable identifiers or digests where supported. For hosted models, select and record the most specific supported version identifier and the version actually served; do not assume a hosted model can be verified by a customer-visible weight digest. Re-evaluate provider or model changes before restoring autonomous approval. Pin dependencies, base images, model version IDs, and tool servers by digest/hash.  2\. Validate SLSA provenance and signatures during deployment; admission controllers reject unsigned or unpinned components.  3\. Require human code-owner approval on the source-control platform for dependency digest updates. |
| **Capacity and abuse limits** | Covers the potential overloading of software-executed and human-executed systems. Bound pipeline load with per-author and per-repository rate limits, global concurrency and cost ceilings, bounded queues, and alerts on queue age and human-review backlog. Overload defers work or routes it through controlled human-review intake; approval requirements never change under load.   **Preconditions:** Limits, queue bounds, and scheduling rules are defined in the protected decision controls policy.  **Postconditions:** Excess work is deferred or rejected according to policy; operators receive threshold alerts; all approvals still require the same checks.  | D-3 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator for admission and scheduling; Reviewer infrastructure for resource isolation, budget enforcement, and queue metrics.  **Algorithm:** 1\. Meter request rate, open reviews, running jobs, and cost per author, per repository, and globally. 2\. Schedule using trusted risk tiers and fairness rules so no tier can monopolize capacity or be starved.  3\. At a limit, defer or reject work, or request human review through a separately bounded queue; never bypass a gate.  4\. Alert on queue age, budget use, and human backlog; apply policy-defined expiry or cancellation to stale work.  |

### 6.5 Audit, Detection, and Response Controls

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Tamper-evident decision logging** | Every decision (approve, veto, or route to a human) produces an immutable record: change identifier and head commit, diff digest, risk tier, each signal's finding and short rationale, each check and model version (with base model and provider), the policy version, each signal's responsible control owner, timestamp, and a digest plus an access-controlled snapshot reference or retained source version for retrieved tool and context data. Store records in write-once storage the reviewer cannot alter or delete; minimize retained sensitive data and enforce retention and access policy. Every approval produces an immutable record: change identifier, diff summary, risk tier, classifier signals, AI reasoning summary, timestamp, and model version — in write-once storage the reviewer cannot modify. **Preconditions:** Append-only decision storage bucket with retention lock is accessible. **Postconditions:** Decision record is immutably stored and hash-chained before any approval token is posted. | R-1, R-2, R-3 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (Object Lock storage, OpenTelemetry, OCSF log exporters). **Algorithm:**  1\. Construct the structured decision payload with the reviewed head commit, diff digest, policy version, per-signal findings and short rationales, check/model versions, control owners, timestamp, and protected references and digests for retained context evidence. Construct structured decision payload (commit SHA, policy version, classifier signals, model ID, reasoning summary).  2\. Write record to immutably locked storage bucket with retention lock (append-only permissions).  3\. Verify write acknowledgment prior to exercising approval authority. |
| **Detection & response integration** | Feed anomalous approval patterns, classifier failures, and service events into standard D\&R tooling. **Preconditions:** SIEM integration is operational outside reviewer runtime control. **Postconditions:** Security ops receive immediate alerts on anomalous agent behaviors or credential misuse. | T-5, S-1, S-2, T-9 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (SIEM log forwarder, alert rules Engine). **Algorithm:**  1\. Stream decision events and service metrics directly to SIEM via log forwarder outside reviewer runtime control.  2\. Run anomaly detections (volume spikes, missing decision logs, adversarial hits) in security team tooling.  3\. Trigger alert channels or automatic Kill switch on high-severity detections. |
| **Owner notification** | Notify code owners of AI-approved changes to their files, with configurable cadence (per-approval to periodic digest). **Preconditions:** Code-ownership mapping and notification channels are active. **Postconditions:** Owners are notified; flagging a change automatically opens an audit ticket and initiates post-merge sampling. | R-1, E-4 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, resolving code-owner contacts. **Algorithm:**  1\. Identify file owners via the code-ownership file.  2\. Query policy for notification cadence per tier.  3\. Dispatch direct notification or batch digest with decision record link and flag action button; log and alert delivery failures without dropping silently. |
| **Kill switch** | An operator-controlled mechanism immediately suspends all approval authority — no approvals clear after activation. Triggerable manually and automatically on defined anomaly signals; re-enablement requires explicit human action (no self-resume). The response runbook covers identifying and, where needed, reverting AI-approved changes merged during the affected window (the rollback capability Section 7 requires). **Preconditions:** Kill switch feature flag or platform token revocation credentials configured. **Postconditions:** Autonomous approvals halt globally or per-repo; system falls back to mandatory human review. | All — containment | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform (app revocation / branch protection overrides) and Review orchestrator feature flags. **Algorithm:**  1\. Monitor manual switch flag or automated trigger criteria.  2\. Immediately withhold approval submissions at orchestrator level or revoke app installations via platform API to halt approvals regardless of reviewer state.  3\. Require authenticated human sign-off to clear the flag. |

### 6.6 Assurance and Continuous Validation

| Control | Description | Mitigates | Example Implementation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Shadow mode before authority** | Before real approval authority is granted in any scope, the system runs silently — recording what it would have decided while humans continue reviewing — and authority expands only when shadow data demonstrates sufficient accuracy. **Preconditions:** Repository mode is set to shadow in policy. **Postconditions:** System generates validation analytics while preventing any automated approvals. | A-1 through A-7 | **Enforced by:** The Governance artifacts (policy mode setting) and Source-control platform permissions. **Algorithm:**  1\. Run full review pipeline and log hypothetical decision records without posting approval (mode controlled via human-owned policy setting; platform prevents approval identity from qualifying in shadow/advisory mode).  2\. Execute offline job comparing agent decisions against human reviewer actions and post-merge metrics.  3\. Require security sign-off PR on policy file to promote scope from shadow to autonomous. |
| **Risk-weighted human sampling** | A subset of AI-approved changes receives human review, sampled at higher rates for higher-risk tiers, generating labeled data and ongoing accuracy measurement. **Preconditions:** Sampling rates per tier are defined in policy. **Postconditions:** Sampled changes generate human review tasks; disagreements initiate audit workflows. | A-1 through A-7, E-4, E-5, T-8, T-9 | **Enforced by:** The Review orchestrator, executing pseudorandom sampling routines. **Algorithm:**  1\. Evaluate tier sampling rate against pseudorandom generator. 2\. Assign sampled PRs to human reviewers (part of the sample in blind mode, with the AI verdict hidden, to compare human and AI review).  3\. Store human evaluation outcome alongside decision record; alert on overdue sample reviews and trip Kill switch if threshold is exceeded. |
| **Adversarial change pipeline** | Synthetic changes containing seeded vulnerabilities — from obvious backdoors to subtle logic and compliance flaws, including flaws split across several PRs — are injected on a recurring cadence; any approval of a seeded change is a concrete gap signal. **Preconditions:** Seeded PR generator harness is active with curated flaw library. **Postconditions:** Seeded approvals cause immediate kill switch activation and security paging. | T-1, T-2, E-5, T-8, T-9, A-2 through A-4 | **Enforced by:** The Reviewer infrastructure (adversarial test harness service). **Algorithm:**  1\. Automatically open PRs containing seeded vulnerabilities against test/mirror repositories via external harness.  2\. Monitor decision log outcomes.  3\. Immediately page owner, open gap ticket, and trip Kill switch for affected scope until human re-enables if a seeded flaw is approved. |
| **Red team exercises** | Recurring human-led exercises against the full system (orchestrator, classifiers, infrastructure) probe for novel attack chains and emergent failure modes; findings feed back into this threat model. **Preconditions:** Red team engagement scope and canary targets are established. **Postconditions:** Threat model and continuous evaluation suites are updated with exercise findings. | All | **Enforced by:** The Governance artifacts (assurance plan policy requiring open finding resolution). **Algorithm:**  1\. Execute red team scenarios against canary reviewer deployments according to human-owned assurance plan.  2\. File identified gaps as security issues.  3\. Gate policy authority expansions on issue resolution (block PRs expanding policy authority while high-severity findings remain open). |
| **Continuous evaluation suite** | Holistic metrics — bug detection accuracy, vulnerability detection, compliance classification accuracy, agreement with human reviewers — tracked over time to detect drift and regression. **Preconditions:** Labelled evaluation dataset is maintained in governance repository. **Postconditions:** Metric regressions block governance updates and alert system owners. | A-1, A-3, T-6, T-9 | **Enforced by:** The Source-control platform via required status checks on governance PRs. **Algorithm:**  1\. Run full review pipeline against labelled benchmark PR dataset on CI trigger or schedule.  2\. Calculate detection, false-positive, and false-negative metrics.  3\. Block governance PR merges via required status checks if accuracy metrics drop below baseline; alert owners and optionally trip Kill switch on scheduled run regressions. 4\. Silent-reviewer test: run the pipeline with every model stubbed to return no findings, over the labelled data set and a recent window of real changes, and report what would have been approved. This set is the organization's exposure to T-9, and the policy owner reviews it before any expansion of eligibility. |

## 7\. Residual Risk and Operating Assumptions

1. **No detection layer is complete.** Classifiers and analyzers reduce, but do not eliminate, the probability that adversarial or flawed changes pass review. Compensating post-merge controls (anomaly monitoring, sampling, rollback capability) are required, not optional. Changes split across several PRs (T-8) are a known gap in per-PR review.  
2. **The AI reviewer must never be the sole control for regulated change.** Where regulation requires human approval, the AI assists; it does not approve.  
3. **Authority must be earned incrementally.** Approval scope expands one tier or code area at a time, gated on shadow-mode and sampling evidence — never granted broadly at launch.  
4. **The threat model is a living artifact.** Red-team findings, seeded-change escapes, and incident learnings must drive revisions on a defined cadence.  
5. **No model is trusted.** The reviewer, the classifiers, and any checker can fail together, especially where they share a base model, provider, or context.

```
Orch->>Ana: Execute Test & Invariant Gate

Orch->>Class: 4. Code Quality Classifier (Rubric Evaluation)
Class-->>Orch: Quality Score / Findings
Orch->>Class: 5. Intent Classifier (Dual-Call & Fact-Check)
Class-->>Orch: Mismatch Verdict / Veto
Orch->>Class: 6. Project-Context Evaluation (REVIEW_CONTEXT.md)
Class-->>Orch: Context Compliance Verdict
Orch->>AI: Request Primary Code Review (Bugs & Correctness)
AI->>Tools: Query External/Internal Context
Tools-->>AI: Data/References
AI-->>Orch: Structured JSON Review Findings & Reasoning
Orch->>Orch: Verify Reviewer Report (Coverage, Grounding, Consistency)
end

%% Final Decision Logic
alt Hard Veto or Gate Failure
Orch->>Orch: Block Autonomous Approval & Route to Human
else All Gates & Checks Passed
Orch->>Appr: Exercise Approval Authority
end
```
